title: Body fluid exposure: first response and reporting
audience: Cleaning and support workers who could meet blood or other body fluids while cleaning, handling linen or waste, or helping with toileting or washing.
learningOutcomes: Put the first-response steps in order after blood or other body fluids reaches the eyes, mouth or skin.
List the details an incident report for a body fluid exposure must include.
Explain why the supervisor must hear about an exposure straight away.

instruction.heading: What counts as an exposure
instruction.body: The guide names blood, urine, sputum, mucus, faeces, semen, vaginal fluid and vomit as body fluids that carry risk. Exposure can happen during toileting, showering, bed bathing, changing catheter bags, cleaning up a body fluid spill, sharp injuries, wound management, brushing teeth or feeding. Treat any contact with these fluids as an exposure until your supervisor tells you otherwise. Sharp injuries are covered in “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”, and this lesson covers splashes and contact with the eyes, mouth and skin.

instruction.heading: First response on the skin, eyes and mouth
instruction.body: Where fluid has reached the skin, wash the exposed area thoroughly using soap and water. If the eyes are affected, rinse them with tap water or saline while holding the eyelids open, and do not rub them. If fluid gets into the mouth, spit it out and keep rinsing until none is left. Take off any soiled clothing and have a shower if it is needed. Move away from the source of the splash first if that is needed to make the area safe.

instruction.heading: Instruments, reporting and documentation
instruction.body: Rinse or wipe any used instrument promptly so that it is ready for reprocessing. Report the exposure verbally to the right person straight away, so that the workplace can decide whether further steps are required. Documentation may then be required of you. A serious exposure calls for an incident report. It should record the events, who was involved, who saw it, where it happened and how far any injury extends, the object responsible for the injury, the kind of fluid, and how much of it reached the worker.

instruction.heading: Why speed matters
instruction.body: Blood-borne viruses such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV can be transmitted through contact with blood. Prompt reporting lets the employer arrange counselling, testing and treatment where these are needed. Decisions about testing timing, follow-up and treatment belong to clinicians and the workplace occupational health process. Keep the identity of the source person private, and share it only with those who need it for the response.

procedure: Step away from the splash if the spot is unsafe, and pause the job.
Wash exposed skin using soap and water.
Rinse the eyes with tap water or saline, with the eyelids held open, if the eyes are affected.
If fluid has entered the mouth, spit it out and rinse repeatedly.
Take off soiled clothing and wash if needed.
Tell the supervisor or nurse in charge verbally straight away, then complete the incident report with the details listed in the lesson.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is mopping after a patient vomited and some of the vomit splashes onto the cleaner face.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is done first, and what is reported?
workedExamples.reasoning: Step out of the splash zone if needed, rinse the eyes with tap water or saline while holding the lids apart, and flush the mouth if fluid got in. Take off soiled clothing and wash the skin using soap and water. Then tell the nurse in charge and the supervisor, and complete the incident report with the details.

workedExamples.situation: A worker assisting with a bed bath has urine splashed onto a bare forearm.
workedExamples.reasoning: Treat it as an exposure: wash the skin using soap and water and tell the supervisor. Complete the incident report. The employer decides on any further action, and the worker does not decide alone that the event is minor.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves, gown or apron, and eye protection or face shield for splash risk
Soap, water and paper towel for skin washing
Tap water or saline for eye rinsing
Incident report form or the workplace reporting system

commonErrors.error: Waiting to see whether the exposure passes before acting.
commonErrors.prevention: Start the first response at once and report straight away.

commonErrors.error: Rubbing the eyes after a splash.
commonErrors.prevention: Rinse with the eyelids held open and do not rub.

commonErrors.error: Reporting only informally, or holding the report until the shift is over.
commonErrors.prevention: Report verbally at once and complete the written record.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not treat yourself beyond the first response. Contact medical help as the workplace procedure says.
Keep the identity of the source person confidential, and share it only with the people who need it for the response.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner sequences the first response for eyes, mouth and skin in the correct order.
Learner lists at least five details an incident report must include.
Learner states that the report is verbal first and written second, and names the supervisor as the first contact.
documentationEvidence: Incident report recording date and time, what happened, who was involved, who witnessed it, where it occurred and how far any injury reaches, the item involved, the kind of body fluid and the quantity of exposure.
summary: After a splash, start the first response at once, rinse the eyes with the lids held open, and do not rub.
Report verbally straight away and complete the written incident report.
Testing and treatment decisions belong to clinicians and the occupational health process.

knowledgeChecks.question: A splash reaches a worker eye. What is the first action?
options: Rub the eye to clear it with a clean cloth and some water
Rinse the eye with tap water or saline with the eyelids held open
Wait until the shift is over and then see the nurse for a check
Apply an alcohol rub to the eye and then wash the hands

knowledgeChecks.question: Which detail belongs in an incident report for a body fluid exposure?
options: The worker favourite cleaning product and the brand of the shampoo
The kind of body fluid and how much of it reached the worker
The weather on the day and the time the cleaning began
The name of the worker previous employer and the shift number

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a body fluid exposure be reported straight away?
options: So that the employer can arrange follow-up advice and testing where needed
So the cleaner can avoid the rest of the shift and go home early
Because reports are only accepted in the first hour and only by the first person
So the cleaner can be paid more and get a bonus for the report
